items.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
items.content: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering:  (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? items.title: Solving a 31-year-old grand challenge in mathematics – the KLS conjecture
items.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension.  Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification.  For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The researcher “then deputized an orchestrator agent to carry out the plan, spinning up agents to do pen-and-paper math, write Lean, and handle support functions like checking that things were staying on track… the execution phase required little scaffolding beyond the initial plan and some agent skills distilled from earlier internal autoformalization efforts.” $135k for math formalization: The work took about a week, taking “on the order of 100B input tokens (90% cache reads) and about 300 million output tokens (totaling an estimated $135,000 in token spend), and produced about 600k lines of Lean.” Now that they’ve done this, they’ve been able to accelerate some other aspects of their research: “We have already seen both benefits from autoformalization in using this library to extend parts of singular learning theory. items.content: Watch the full episode on YouTube As we learned from the Anthropic S-1 filings yesterday , the lab has some of the highest revenue and research efficiency in human history, particularly with -126% loss to 19% GAAP profit turnaround in the last year. The company credits this to their two core loops: Improvement and Investment: Today we go inside how Anthropic works. Now the dust has settled on Opus 5.5 and it has lasted a month as the generally accepted #1 LLM in the world, we dive into its launch, and how Anthropic ships Claude with Claude with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang , heads of Engineering and Product respectively. The team is working under two kinds of pressure. The models are getting more capable, which makes safe deployment and access decisions harder. At the same time, usage is growing fast enough that ordinary infrastructure choices—like how much CPU an API consumes—become strategic. Those problems meet in the product choices that reach developers. A model launch is also an API launch Anthropic's Opus 5.5 launch emphasizes both model quality and cost. We discuss feedback that the previous Opus generations were be too verbose, alongside the need for stronger intelligence per dollar. Anthropic says the new model costs less to run than its predecessor; the exact saving depends on the workload and its use of cached context. The less visible launch work involves changes to how people integrate the API. One example we discuss is protecting model reasoning against extraction used for distillation. Preserving thinking blocks across turns helps address this, but a new requirement can also break a customer's existing harness. Katelyn also describes what being part of early access programs actually looks like in practice: Customers run evaluations in their own harnesses, report surprising behavior, and sometimes pass along less formal impressions. items.title: Coding From the Himalayas With an Offline AI Agent
items.content: When we talk about working remotely , we take a lot of things for granted, especially reliable internet and power. But sometimes, working remotely means trying to get something done on a flight, during a long train ride, or somewhere with little or no network. I moved to the foothills of the Himalayas a year ago. I love the peace of living here, but it also comes with its own challenges, including network and power outages . Things I didn’t think about as much before are now part of planning my work. I work as a Principal Engineer at Thomson Reuters , where I spend most of my time coding and reviewing my teammates’ code. Coding agents are already a big part of my everyday workflow, which made me curious about how much of that workflow I could keep using offline. Working from the foothills of the Himalayas. Photo of my workspace. If you’re someone like me, who enjoys working with technology but also finds peace in quiet, remote places where the network doesn’t always cooperate, this article is for you. It’s also for anyone who has wondered whether a coding agent can run entirely on their laptop, with the internet switched off. I tried running a coding agent locally on my laptop to see how much work I could actually get done offline. What can we do offline? A project already on your laptop gives us plenty to work with. We can ask an agent to explain an unfamiliar function, investigate a failing test, refactor a small piece of code, or help finish a feature. These tasks can run offline when the model, project dependencies and test tools are available locally. Downloading a new package or looking something up on the web will still need a connection. Where OpenCode fits OpenCode is an open-source coding agent that works with your project. You give it a task, and it can read files, propose edits and run commands such as the test suite. In our setup, its permission prompts let us review commands and changes before allowing them. I picked OpenCode because it lets me keep t…

items.content: Today is one of those days that is tougher to cover for a normally-engineer audience that isn’t used to reading most S-1’s, let alone 350 pages of one of the most unusual S-1’s of all time : Better visualized: With significant operating leverage causing the first profitable quarter in Anthropic history (adjusted for $1B/quarter of SBC): The incredible efficiency story is told in two loops, and of course you know, we love loop: The pitch going forward is “virtual collaborators” (don’t say agent!) for over a billion knowledge workers by 2028: We believe we have reached an inflection point where AI systems can function as genuine collaborators in professional work. They quickly complete substantive tasks that might otherwise occupy a skilled professional for several hours, a full day, or longer. AI systems are also becoming increasingly capable of performing tasks that were previously too difficult or costly to complete or surfacing original insights and analyses. We refer to these AI systems that work alongside humans to perform complex, multi-step work at professional levels as Virtual Collaborators. Virtual Collaborators carry the access rights, system connections, and context that their organizations grant them , which allows them to function more accurately and reliably. They can navigate and use internal tools and execute workflows that span multiple steps that require sustained reasoning. Virtual Collaborators are AI designed to be embedded where work gets done, and our aim is to continue extending them to knowledge workers globally, a population that is estimated to exceed one billion in 2028. And we end with a useful map of all of Anthropic’s offerings on one screen: AI Twitter Recap Top Story: Anthropic files its S-1. items.title: Take Ten-Thousand: Egocentric Data Collection for Humanoid Robots
items.content: The ChinaTalk team is going to CoRL (the Conference on Robot Learning) in Austin! Reply to this email if you’d like to hang out between November 9th and 12th. We’re also doing karaoke on the 11th — RSVP here if you’d like to join! A. Chen writes about people, technologies, and their relationships to power. Her submission, “Take Ten-Thousand: Egocentric Data Collection for Humanoid Robots,” won one of 7 Grand Prizes at the ChinaTalk Essay Contest. We’re thrilled to share this report from the frontlines of China’s robot data collection industry! Where is the center of the universe? For the residents of Beijing, the answer is Wudaokou. The neighborhood houses China’s top universities, research institutions, and labs, drawing talent and funding from every corner of the country. The streets are radiant at night, packed full of bars and clubs that have somehow bounced back after the COVID-19 pandemic. And the number 13 metro line, which rattles overhead every five minutes, is never empty. I came to Wudaokou to understand China’s AI industry — particularly, the hype surrounding humanoid robots, and the methods used to train them. Everyone has seen videos of these robots: eerily tall and lanky, some of them shedding nuts and bolts as they sprint down a track, others backflipping repeatedly on a dance stage. The global market for humanoid robotics, or embodied intelligence, is said to be worth $38 billion by 2035: the latest chapter in the U.S.-China technology race that has dominated international headlines for over a decade. This year, China’s 15 th Five-Year Plan declared embodied intelligence a matter of national priority, then laid a strategy for developing training grounds across the country. Over 150 humanoid robotics companies and 40 state-owned robot data collection centers were reported to be in operation in China by the end of 2025. items.title: MOFCOM's New Rules and the Future of Chinese AI
items.content: In the AI race thus far, openness has been China’s secret sauce. As fast followers to the frontier, Chinese AI companies have gained trust by publicizing their weights and architectures. And at the cost of revenue, they have achieved global adoption, brand recognition, and a truly competitive dynamic with American labs. Last week, China’s Ministries of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Science and Technology (MOST) jointly proposed expanding China’s catalogue of export-controlled technologies, with most of the proposed regulations taking aim at subsets of China’s AI industry. Regulators will spend a month taking comments on the draft before anything becomes law, but we can already learn a ton from this announcement in its current form. Does Beijing want to hold back the tides of open models? Why is MOFCOM writing these rules now, and what does this say about the Chinese government’s appetite for AI-enabled risks versus growth? To find out, we spent three days poring over the draft regulations — so you don’t have to! What’s ahead: How these rules came to be — and how this draft is already affecting the Chinese AI industry; What the proposed rules mean for frontier models, chip design, memory, cybersecurity, AI content detection, and even China’s minority languages; Who actually decides which export licenses get approved, and the balance of power between provincial and central authorities; What these rules tell us about Beijing’s expectations for AI development. The 40 proposed additions in Announcement 48, split across AI, photovoltaics, and biomedicine. Today, we’re just focusing on the AI-related regulations, but a future piece tackling everything else — from this announcement’s proposed restrictions on PV cells and gene therapies, to other recent announcements on port dredgers and tunnel borers — is in the works!
